source_refs.note: Practice long questions written from Chapter 16 (PDF 61-84, printed 1-24); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 16 (Electrostatics / Static Electricity), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define electric potential difference and its SI unit. Write the relation between electric field and potential difference, explain the meaning of its negative sign, and obtain the form it takes for a uniform field. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: Electric potential difference between two points is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between them. If a test charge q₀ is moved from A to B in a uniform field (Fig. 16.1):
V = V_B − V_A = W_AB/q₀ = ΔU/q₀ ... (16.1)

Unit: the SI unit is the volt: 1 V = 1 J/1 C ... (16.2). It can be scaled to kilovolts or millivolts.

Relation with electric field: the potential changes with distance in the field as
ΔV = −E Δd ... (16.3)
so the electric field is the (negative) rate of change of potential with distance:
E = −ΔV/Δd ... (16.4)

Negative sign: it indicates that the field points from higher to lower potential; the potential decreases in the direction of the field.

Uniform field: for a uniform field between two plates a distance d apart with potential difference V, the magnitude is
E = V/d ... (16.5)
So the potential difference between two points is directly proportional to the field strength and to the distance between them; a stronger field causes a more rapid decrease in potential.

book_ref.quote: The electric potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between two points

blocks.prompt: 2 Two parallel plates 0.8 cm apart are connected to a 24 V battery. Find (i) the electric field between the plates, (ii) the force on a charge of 5 μC placed between them, and (iii) the work done in moving this charge from one plate to the other. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use E = V/d for the uniform field, F = qE, and W = qV from the definition of potential difference.

book_ref.quote: In the case of a uniform electric field, this relation simplifies to:

blocks.prompt: 3 Define electric potential at a point. Derive an expression for the electric potential at a distance r from a positive point charge q. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: The electric potential at a point in an electric field is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point, keeping it in electrostatic equilibrium. V = W/q₀ ... (16.6). It is a scalar.

Derivation: ΔV = −E Δr needs a constant E, but the field of a point charge is radial and E varies as 1/r². So take two points A and B, infinitesimally close, at distances r_A and r_B from q (Fig. 16.2), so that E is almost constant between them:
r_B = r_A + Δr ... (16.7), Δr = r_B − r_A ... (16.8)
The midpoint of AB is at r = (r_A + r_B)/2 ... (16.9), where
E = (1/4πε₀)(q/r²) ... (16.10)
As A and B are very close, the arithmetic mean is taken equal to the geometric mean:
r² = r_A r_B ... (16.11)
E = (1/4πε₀)(q/r_A r_B) ... (16.12)
Work done in moving a unit positive charge from B to A equals the potential difference:
V_A − V_B = −E(r_A − r_B) = E(r_B − r_A) ... (16.13)
Substituting E from (16.12):
V_A − V_B = (q/4πε₀)((r_B − r_A)/(r_A r_B)) ... (16.14)
V_A − V_B = (q/4πε₀)(1/r_A − 1/r_B) ... (16.15)

Absolute potential: take B at infinity, so V_B = 0 and 1/r_B = 1/∞ = 0:
V_A = (1/4πε₀)(q/r_A) ... (16.16)
In general, at distance r: V_r = (1/4πε₀)(q/r) ... (16.17)
The potential is negative for a negative charge; for several charges the total potential is the algebraic sum of the individual potentials.

book_ref.quote: Let us take two points A and B, infinitesimally close to each other, so that E remains almost constant between them.

blocks.prompt: 4 Point charges of +4 nC and −6 nC are placed 50 cm apart. Find (i) the electric potential at the midpoint of the line joining them, and (ii) the point between them where the potential is zero. (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Potential is a scalar: add the two potentials with their signs; for the zero point, set the magnitudes equal.

book_ref.quote: the total electric potential is the algebraic sum of the individual potentials created by all the charges

steps: Midpoint: r = 0.25 m from each charge; V = (9 × 10⁹)(4 × 10⁻⁹ − 6 × 10⁻⁹)/0.25 = −72 V
Zero point at x from +4 nC: (1/4πε₀)(4 nC/x) = (1/4πε₀)(6 nC/(50 cm − x))
4(50 cm − x) = 6x → 200 cm = 10x → x = 20 cm from the +4 nC charge (30 cm from the −6 nC charge)
blocks.final_answer: (i) V = −72 V; (ii) 20 cm from the +4 nC charge

blocks.prompt: 5 Derive an expression for the electric potential energy of a system of two point charges Q and q separated by a distance r. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Consider two points A and B a distance r apart (Fig. 16.4) where initially there is no electric field.

Step 1: Bring charge Q from infinity to A. There is no field at A, so Q faces no opposition:
W_A = 0 ... (16.19)

Step 2: Q at A creates a potential at B:
V = (1/4πε₀)(Q/r) ... (16.20)
Now bring a second charge q from infinity to B. Work is done against the field of Q:
W_B = q × (electric potential) = qV ... (16.21)
W_B = q(1/4πε₀)(Q/r) = (1/4πε₀)(Qq/r) ... (16.22)

Total work: W = W_A + W_B = 0 + (1/4πε₀)(Qq/r)
W = (1/4πε₀)(Qq/r) ... (16.23)

This work is stored as electric potential energy of the system:
E_p = (1/4πε₀)(Qq/r) ... (16.24)
E_p is in joules; it is inversely proportional to the separation r.

book_ref.quote: The concept of electric potential directly leads to the expression for electric potential energy of two point charges

blocks.prompt: 6 Two point charges of +5 μC and +2 μC are 30 cm apart. Find (i) their electric potential energy, and (ii) the work needed to bring them to 10 cm apart. (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find E_p = (1/4πε₀)(Qq/r) at both separations; the work needed is the increase in potential energy.

book_ref.quote: Two point charges are separated by a distance of 4.0 cm.

blocks.prompt: 7 Explain the motion of positive and negative charges released in an electric field. Show that a charge q₀ of mass m falling through a potential difference ΔV gains speed given by ½mv² = q₀ΔV, and define the electron-volt. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Motion: If a charge q₀ is placed in the field of a charge q and is free to move, it is repelled away. By Eq. (16.17) the potential decreases with distance. So a free positive charge always accelerates from a point of higher potential to a point of lower potential. A free negative charge moves from lower to higher potential.

Energy: If the potential difference between the two points is ΔV, the potential energy of the charge decreases by
ΔU = q₀ΔV
This decrease appears as kinetic energy. If the body of mass m starts from rest and reaches the lower-potential-energy point with velocity v:
½mv² = q₀ΔV ... (16.18)
so v = √(2q₀ΔV/m).

Electron-volt: Eq. (16.18) shows energy can be expressed as charge × potential difference. One electron-volt is the energy acquired by an electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1 volt:
1 eV = charge on an electron × 1 volt = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
It is a unit of energy used in atomic physics.

book_ref.quote: This decrease in potential energy of the charge will appear as its kinetic energy.

blocks.prompt: 8 A particle of mass 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ kg carrying a charge of 4 μC starts from rest and is accelerated through 50 V. Find (i) its kinetic energy, and (ii) its final speed. (iii) What energy, in eV and in joules, would an electron gain through the same 50 V? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The loss of potential energy q₀ΔV becomes kinetic energy ½mv².

book_ref.quote: the body will reach the point at lower potential energy with velocity v

blocks.prompt: 9 What is an isolated spherical conductor? Define its capacitance and the farad, and derive an expression for the capacitance of an isolated sphere of radius R. On what does it depend? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Isolated spherical conductor: a spherical conductor placed in space far from other conductors or influence. Its ability to store charge is its capacitance C.

Definition: the capacitance of an isolated spherical conductor is the charge stored on the sphere per unit electric potential at its surface:
C = Q/V ... (16.25)
SI unit: farad (F). For a sphere, 1 farad is the capacitance of a sphere that stores 1 coulomb when its potential is 1 volt (isolated in free space): 1 F = 1 C/1 V.

Derivation: the charge Q lies on the outer surface. The potential at the surface of a sphere of radius R is
V = (1/4πε₀)(Q/R)
Substituting in (16.25):
C = Q/[(1/4πε₀)(Q/R)]
C = 4πε₀R ... (16.26)
In a medium of dielectric constant εᵣ:
C = 4πε₀εᵣR ... (16.27)

Dependence: C is independent of the charge or potential; it depends on the radius of the sphere and the medium. C increases with radius, so larger spheres store more charge at the same surface potential; a dielectric medium also increases C.

book_ref.quote: defined as the electric charge stored on the sphere per unit electric potential at its surface

blocks.prompt: 10 An isolated metal sphere of radius 27 cm is in air. Find (i) its capacitance, (ii) the charge needed to raise its surface potential to 6000 V, and (iii) its capacitance in a medium of dielectric constant 2.5. (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use C = 4πε₀R = R/(9 × 10⁹), then Q = CV, then multiply C by εᵣ.

book_ref.quote: The capacitance increases with increase in radius of the sphere.

steps: C = 4πε₀R = 0.27 m/(9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²) = 3 × 10⁻¹¹ F = 30 pF

blocks.prompt: 11 Define the capacitance of a capacitor. Derive an expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor (i) with vacuum and (ii) with a dielectric of relative permittivity εᵣ between its plates. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Capacitance: when a capacitor is connected to a battery of voltage V, the plates get +Q and −Q, and Q ∝ V:
Q = CV or C = Q/V ... (16.28)
The capacitance is the amount of charge on one plate needed to raise its potential by one volt with respect to the other. Unit: farad (coulomb per volt).

Derivation (vacuum): two parallel metal plates, each of area A, are a small distance d apart (Fig. 16.6), so the field E between them is uniform and confined between the plates.
C_vac = Q/V ... (16.29)
For a uniform field: E = V/d ... (16.30)
By Gauss's law, E = σ/ε₀, and the surface charge density σ = Q/A, so
E = Q/(Aε₀) ... (16.31)
From (16.30) and (16.31): V/d = Q/(Aε₀), or Q/V = Aε₀/d
C_vac = Q/V = Aε₀/d ... (16.32)

With a dielectric: an insulating material of relative permittivity εᵣ between the plates enhances the capacitance by the factor εᵣ:
C_med = Aε₀εᵣ/d ... (16.33)
So the capacitance depends on the plate area A, the separation d and the medium (εᵣ) between the plates.

book_ref.quote: The distance d is small so that the electric field E between the plates is uniform

blocks.prompt: 12 A parallel plate capacitor has square plates of side 10 cm separated by 0.2 mm of a dielectric of εᵣ = 6. Find (i) its capacitance, and (ii) the charge on each plate when it is connected to a 50 V supply. (Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻².) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find the plate area, use C_med = Aε₀εᵣ/d, then Q = CV.

book_ref.quote: the capacitance of capacitor is enhanced by the factor

blocks.prompt: 13 Describe an experiment showing the effect of inserting a dielectric between the plates of a charged capacitor. Define the dielectric constant and explain, in terms of polarization, why the potential difference between the plates decreases. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Experiment (Fig. 16.7): a charged capacitor is connected to a voltmeter; its deflection measures the potential difference between the plates. When a dielectric material is inserted between the plates, the reading drops, showing that V decreases. Since C = Q/V and Q remains constant, C increases:
C_med = Aε₀εᵣ/d ... (16.33)

Dielectric constant: dividing (16.33) by C_vac = Aε₀/d (16.32):
εᵣ = C_med/C_vac ... (16.34)
It is the ratio of the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with an insulating substance between the plates to its capacitance with vacuum (or air) between them.

Polarization: a dielectric is an insulator with no free electrons; all electrons are bound to their nuclei. In an electric field the electrons of each atom are displaced slightly relative to the nucleus, opposite to the field (Fig. 16.7 c). This is polarization of the dielectric; the distorted atom is polarized.

Why V decreases: in a slab between charged plates, the atoms are polarized by the field (Fig. 16.7 d). Charges appear on the faces of the slab in contact with the plates, with polarity opposite to the adjacent plate. This effectively decreases the charge on the plates, so the electric intensity and the potential difference between the plates decrease.

book_ref.quote: The reason for decrease in potential difference between the plates of the capacitor is the polarization of the atoms

blocks.prompt: 14 A 40 pF air capacitor is charged to 200 V and disconnected from the battery. When a dielectric slab fills the space between the plates, the voltmeter reading falls to 50 V. Find (i) the charge on the plates, (ii) the new capacitance, and (iii) the dielectric constant of the slab. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The capacitor is isolated, so Q stays constant; the new C is Q/V and εᵣ = C_med/C_vac.

book_ref.quote: since V decreases while Q remains constant, the value of C increases

steps: Q = C_vac V = 40 × 10⁻¹² F × 200 V = 8 × 10⁻⁹ C (stays constant)

blocks.prompt: 15 What is meant by combination of capacitors? Explain the parallel combination of three capacitors and derive the formula for their equivalent capacitance. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Combination: when more than one capacitor is connected together in a circuit to obtain a desired capacitance, it is a combination of capacitors; it behaves as a single equivalent capacitor. The two common types are parallel and series.

Parallel combination (Fig. 16.8): the plates on one side of all capacitors are connected to the negative terminal and the plates on the other side to the positive terminal of the battery.
(i) The potential difference V across each capacitor is the same.
(ii) The charge on each is different, depending on its capacitance: Q₁, Q₂, Q₃ on C₁, C₂, C₃.

Derivation: the equivalent capacitor C_e holds the same total charge under the same V:
Q = Q₁ + Q₂ + Q₃
Putting Q₁ = C₁V, Q₂ = C₂V, Q₃ = C₃V and Q = C_eV:
C_eV = C₁V + C₂V + C₃V
C_e = C₁ + C₂ + C₃ ... (16.35)

Result: when capacitors are connected in parallel, their combined capacitance is equal to the sum of their individual capacitances.

book_ref.quote: In this combination the potential difference V across the plates of each capacitor is the same.

blocks.prompt: 16 Capacitors of 2 μF, 4 μF and 6 μF are connected in parallel across a 15 V battery. Find (i) the equivalent capacitance, (ii) the charge on each capacitor, and (iii) the total charge. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: In parallel every capacitor has the full 15 V; add the capacitances and use Q = CV for each.

book_ref.quote: The charge on each will be different depending upon its capacitance.

steps: Q₁ = 2 μF × 15 V = 30 μC; Q₂ = 4 μF × 15 V = 60 μC; Q₃ = 6 μF × 15 V = 90 μC

blocks.prompt: 17 Explain the series combination of three capacitors. Show that each capacitor carries the same charge and derive the formula for their equivalent capacitance. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Arrangement (Fig. 16.9): capacitors are connected one after the other in a line. The second plate of C₁ is joined to the first plate of C₂, the second plate of C₂ to the first plate of C₃; the first plate of C₁ and the second plate of C₃ are connected to the battery.

Same charge: the battery sends +Q to the first plate of C₁. The second plate of C₁ is insulated from the first, so it draws no charge from the battery, but +Q induces an equal −Q on it. Then +Q appears on the first plate of C₂ connected to it, and so on for C₃. So each capacitor has charge of magnitude Q on each plate.

Voltages: the potential difference across the combination equals the battery voltage V, but it is shared according to capacitance:
V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃ ... (16.36)

Derivation: the equivalent capacitor C_e also has charge Q at voltage V. Using V = Q/C:
V = Q/C_e, V₁ = Q/C₁, V₂ = Q/C₂, V₃ = Q/C₃
Putting in (16.36): Q/C_e = Q/C₁ + Q/C₂ + Q/C₃
1/C_e = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + 1/C₃ ... (16.37)

Result: the reciprocal of the equivalent capacitance equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual capacitances.

book_ref.quote: Thus each capacitor receives a charge of magnitude Q on each of its plates.

blocks.prompt: 18 Capacitors of 4 μF, 6 μF and 12 μF are connected in series across a 60 V battery. Find (i) the equivalent capacitance, (ii) the charge on each capacitor, and (iii) the potential difference across each. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Add reciprocals for C_e; the same charge Q = C_eV sits on each; then V = Q/C for each.

book_ref.quote: In series combination charge on each capacitor will be the same Q.

steps: Q = C_eV = 2 μF × 60 V = 120 μC on each capacitor
blocks.final_answer: (i) 2 μF; (ii) 120 μC = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ C on each; (iii) 30 V, 20 V, 10 V

blocks.prompt: 19 Explain why a charged capacitor possesses energy. Using the potential-charge graph, show that the energy stored in a capacitor is ½QV, and express it in terms of C and V. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Why energy: work is done to deposit charge on the plates, and this is stored as electrical potential energy. Evidence: if the plates of a charged capacitor are joined by a thick wire, charge flows to neutralize the plates and the wire becomes hot; this heat is the energy the capacitor had.

Graph: since Q ∝ V, the V vs Q graph is a straight line through the origin (Fig. 16.10). With each small increment of charge, the potential difference rises, so more work is needed for the next increment.

Derivation: divide the area under the graph into small charge increments ΔQ. The work to move ΔQ through the potential difference V₁ across the plates is
ΔW = (ΔQ)(V₁) ... (16.38)
which is the area of a thin rectangle under the graph. The total work to charge the capacitor to Q is the sum of all such rectangles, i.e. the total area under the graph, the right-angled triangle OAB:
Area of triangle OAB = ½(base)(height) = ½(OA)(AB)
With OA = Q (total charge) and AB = V (final potential difference):
Energy stored, W = ½QV ... (16.39)

In terms of C and V: put Q = CV:
W = ½(CV)V = ½CV² ... (16.40)

book_ref.quote: Let us determine the electric potential energy stored in a charged capacitor graphically.

blocks.prompt: 20 A 5 μF capacitor is charged to 600 V. Find (i) the charge on it, (ii) the energy stored, and (iii) the energy stored if it is charged to 1200 V instead. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use Q = CV and W = ½CV²; since W ∝ V², doubling V gives four times the energy.

book_ref.quote: If we put the value of Q = CV in eq. (16.39), we get

blocks.prompt: 21 Show that the energy of a charged parallel plate capacitor can be regarded as stored in the electric field between its plates, and derive the expression for the energy density of an electric field. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Idea: instead of the potential energy of the charges on the plates, the energy can be regarded as stored in the electric field between the plates. This view is useful when the field strength between the plates is to be considered.

Derivation: start from the energy stored, W = ½CV² (16.40), i.e. P.E = ½CV². For a parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric:
C = Aε₀εᵣ/d and, for the uniform field, V = Ed
Substituting:
Energy = ½(Aε₀εᵣ/d)(Ed)²
= ½ε₀εᵣE² × (Ad)
Here (Ad) is the volume between the plates. So the energy per unit volume is
Energy density = Energy/Volume = ½ε₀εᵣE² ... (16.42)

Meaning: the energy density depends only on the field strength E and the medium; this relation is valid for any electric field strength. Unit: J m⁻³.

book_ref.quote: It is also possible to regard the energy as being stored in electric field between the plates

blocks.prompt: 22 An air-filled parallel plate capacitor has plates of area 0.04 m² separated by 2 mm and is connected to a 500 V supply. Find (i) the electric field between the plates, (ii) the energy density, and (iii) the total energy stored between the plates. (Take ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; εᵣ = 1 for air.) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find E = V/d, then energy density ½ε₀E², then multiply by the volume Ad.

book_ref.quote: This equation is valid for any electric field strength.

steps: Energy density = ½ε₀εᵣE² = ½(8.85 × 10⁻¹²)(1)(2.5 × 10⁵)² = 0.277 J m⁻³

blocks.prompt: 23 With the help of an R-C circuit and graphs of charge against time, explain the charging and discharging of a capacitor. Define the time constant and show that the product RC has the unit of time. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
R-C circuit (Fig. 16.11): a resistor R and capacitor C with a switch S.

Charging: with S at A, the R-C combination is connected to a battery V₀, which charges the capacitor through R. The capacitor is not charged immediately: q = 0 at t = 0 and the charge builds up gradually to the equilibrium value q₀ = CV₀ (Fig. 16.12). The voltage at any instant is V = q/C.

Discharging: with S at B (Fig. 16.13 a), the charge +q on the left plate flows anti-clockwise through the resistance and neutralizes −q on the right plate. Discharging begins at t = 0 with q = CV₀ and the charge decreases gradually to zero (Fig. 16.13 b).

Time constant: how fast the capacitor charges or discharges depends on the product RC. As RC has the unit of time it is called the time constant τ = RC; it is the time in which the capacitor deposits 0.63 times the equilibrium charge q₀. A small time constant means the charge reaches equilibrium sooner, and a smaller RC gives a more rapid discharge.

Unit of RC: from Ohm's law V = IR and I = q/t: V = (q/t)R, so R = Vt/q. From q = CV: C = q/V.
RC = (Vt/q)(q/V) = t
Hence 1 ohm × 1 farad = 1 second.

book_ref.quote: Many electric circuits consist of both capacitors and resistors.

blocks.prompt: 24 A 4 μF capacitor is charged through a 500 kΩ resistor from a 9 V battery. Find (i) the time constant, (ii) the equilibrium charge, and (iii) the charge and the voltage across the capacitor after one time constant. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: τ = RC; the final charge is q₀ = CV₀; after one time constant the charge is 0.63 q₀ and V = q/C.

book_ref.quote: defined as the time required by the capacitor to deposit 0.63 times the equilibrium charge

blocks.prompt: 25 Write the exponential decay equation for the charge of a capacitor discharging through a resistor. Show that after one time constant the charge falls to about 0.37 Q₀, and derive the time t½ in which the charge falls to half its initial value. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Decay equation: for a discharging capacitor, any quantity x (charge, voltage or current) decays as
x = x₀e^(−t/RC) ... (16.43)
so Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC), V = V₀e^(−t/RC) and I = I₀e^(−t/RC), where e ≈ 2.718 and RC = τ is the time constant. The negative exponent shows the quantity decreases exponentially: fast at first, then more slowly.

After one time constant: put t = RC:
Q = Q₀e^(−RC/RC) = Q₀e⁻¹ = Q₀/e = Q₀/2.718 = 0.37 Q₀
So the time constant is the time in which the initial charge Q₀ drops to about 0.37 Q₀ (37%); voltage and current drop to the same extent. A smaller τ means a faster response, a larger τ a slower one.

Half time: put Q = ½Q₀ in the decay equation:
½Q₀ = Q₀e^(−t½/RC), or ½ = e^(−t½/RC)
By definition of natural logarithm: ln(½) = −t½/RC
t½ = −(RC) ln(½) ... (16.44)
Now ln(½) = ln 1 − ln 2 = 0 − ln 2 = −0.693 ≈ −0.69
t½ = −RC(−0.69)
t½ = 0.69 RC ... (16.45)
(Fig. 16.16: the charge falls to ½Q₀ at 0.69RC and to 0.37Q₀ at RC.)

book_ref.quote: If we put t = RC, we will get the quantity of charge remained after 1 time constant.

blocks.prompt: 26 A 400 μF capacitor charged to 15 V discharges through a 5 kΩ resistor. Find (i) the time constant, (ii) the time in which the voltage falls to half, and (iii) the voltage after 4 s. (e = 2.718) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: τ = RC; t½ = 0.69 RC; then V = V₀e^(−t/RC).

book_ref.quote: Determine the voltage across the capacitor after 0.2 s.

blocks.prompt: 27 Explain the use of capacitors in (i) electric fans and motors, (ii) a camera flashgun, (iii) refrigerators and air conditioners, and (iv) the medical field. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Electric fans and motors: a capacitor is connected to the starting of the fan motor and charges when power is switched on. It shifts the phase of the current in the starting coil relative to the running coil, so the two coils produce a rotating magnetic field, which gives the motor its starting torque and the fan begins spinning. (It does not supply extra power.) Capacitors play the same role in motors of washing machines, blenders, choppers, grinders and water drawing motors.

(ii) Flashgun: the capacitor charges from the camera battery. When the shutter button is pressed it is connected to the flash tube containing xenon gas. Its rapid discharge provides the high current that ionizes the xenon, which emits a burst of bright light.

(iii) Refrigerators and air conditioners: their compressors use single-phase motors that can struggle to start on their own, so a high-capacitance start capacitor is used. Once the motor reaches a certain speed a relay disconnects it. A run capacitor stays connected to improve energy efficiency. A capacitor with a resistor forms a time delay circuit that delays triggering the power supply, protecting the device from power fluctuation.

(iv) Medical field: capacitors store the energy for a life-saving shock to the heart in cardiac arrest; in imaging machines (CT, MRI, X-ray, ultrasound) they filter out noise and improve image clarity; in EEG and ECG machines they filter out unwanted signals.

Capacitors are also widely used in rectification (converting AC into DC).

book_ref.quote: Capacitors are used in various household appliances such as electric fans

blocks.prompt: 28 The capacitor of a flashgun has a capacitance of 400 μF and is charged to 250 V. Find (i) the charge stored, (ii) the energy available for the flash, and (iii) the energy available if the capacitor is charged only to 125 V. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: The flash gets the energy stored in the capacitor: Q = CV and W = ½CV²; halving V gives a quarter of the energy.

book_ref.quote: In a flashgun, a capacitor stores and releases electrical energy to power the flash tube.
